title: Connect Four
description: Two-color gravity grid. `drop(col, color)` settles into the lowest empty row; `winner()` scans the 6×7 board for any 4-in-a-row in the four directions (→, ↑, ↗, ↘).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Build Connect Four. `drop(col, color)` places a piece at the lowest empty row of `col`, returning the row it landed at. `winner()` returns 'R' or 'Y' if four-in-a-row exists, else ''. Let me confirm a few things:"

• Board size — standard 6 rows × 7 cols?
• Row indexing — is row 0 the bottom of the board (gravity drops settle at low row indices) or the top?
• What does `drop` return on a full column — a sentinel like -1, or throw?
• Colors — fixed to 'R'/'Y' or arbitrary strings? Empty cells — `''` or `null`?
• Do I need to enforce turn alternation, or is the caller responsible?
sections.why: The row-orientation question is critical — it determines whether `drop` scans from low row to high or vice versa. Picking and stating the convention upfront prevents the mid-implementation confusion of 'wait, which way is up?'. Outsourcing turn enforcement to the caller is also worth surfacing — it keeps the class focused on board mechanics, not game state.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(rows × cols) winner check before you discard it.
sections.say:
"The obvious `winner()` is: scan every cell on the board; for each non-empty cell, probe in all 8 directions counting consecutive same-color pieces; if any direction hits 4, return that color. That's O(rows × cols × 8 × 4) = O(rows × cols) per call.

There's an optimization: you don't need all 8 directions. The reverse of every direction would re-detect the same line from its other end, so 4 vectors (→, ↑, ↗, ↘) suffice — that's the canonical.

A further optimization: after a `drop`, you only need to check the 4 lines passing through the just-dropped cell. That cuts winner-after-drop from O(rows × cols) to O(1). But it requires `drop` to know about win-checking — couples the two methods. The full-scan keeps the API clean."
sections.why: Surfacing both the 4-vs-8 directions optimization AND the local-vs-global win check shows you see the layered choices. The interviewer might push you toward the local-check version mid-interview ('what if the board were 1000x1000?') — having pre-surfaced it means you've already done that pivot mentally.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: Why is 'count 4 consecutive in 4 directions' the right shape?
sections.say:
"This is a 'directional run-length on a grid' problem. The key insight is that any winning configuration is 4 colinear cells in one of 4 lines: horizontal, vertical, slash-diagonal, backslash-diagonal. So the search space per cell is exactly 4 direction vectors `[[0,1],[1,0],[1,1],[1,-1]]`, and for each direction I count consecutive same-color matches up to 4.

Why 4 not 8? Because every direction has an inverse — if I check `(0, 1)` (rightward) from cell A, I'd find the same 4-line when starting from cell B four steps to the right and checking `(0, -1)` (leftward). Dropping the inverses halves the work with no loss of coverage.

The walk itself is bounded — `while (k < 4)`, breaking on bounds or mismatch. So each cell-direction pair does O(1) work, total O(rows × cols × 4) = O(rows × cols).

The drop function is even simpler: a column-walk from row 0 upward, settling on the first `''` cell. Linear in column height. The 'is column full?' pre-check is implicit in the `return -1` sentinel after the loop."
sections.why: Naming '4 directions because inverses are redundant' is the structural answer — most candidates either guess 8 (correct but wasteful) or 4 (correct without justification). The third path — explaining why — is what differentiates. The directional run-length framing also generalizes to Gomoku, word search in a grid, ship placement detection — same template.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace three games — two drops with no winner yet, a horizontal R win, and a vertical Y win. Result format: each drop returns the row it landed at, winner returns the color string or ''."

examples.note: Two pieces, no run of 4 anywhere — winner returns ''.
examples.trace:
drop(0,R): r=0 of col 0 is '' → place 'R', return 0
drop(1,Y): r=0 of col 1 is '' → place 'Y', return 0
winner(): scan (0,0)='R'. 4 dirs:
  →: k=1 try (0,1)='Y' ≠ R, break. k=1.
  ↑: k=1 try (1,0)='' ≠ R, break.
  ↗: k=1 try (1,1)='' ≠ R, break.
  ↘: k=1 try (1,-1) OOB, break.
  no dir reaches k=4. scan (0,1)='Y' similarly. nothing. return ''

examples.note: 4 R's in the bottom row → horizontal win in direction →.
examples.trace:
After 4 drops, row 0 = ['R','R','R','R','','','']
winner(): scan (0,0)='R'. dir → (0,1):
  k=1 (0,1)='R' match, k=2
  k=2 (0,2)='R' match, k=3
  k=3 (0,3)='R' match, k=4. STOP.
  k===4 → return 'R'

examples.note: Vertical stack in column 0 → ↑ direction wins.
examples.trace:
drops return 0,1,2,3 (filling col 0 bottom-up)
col 0 = ['Y','Y','Y','Y','','']
winner(): scan (0,0)='Y'. dir ↑ (1,0):
  k=1 (1,0)='Y', k=2
  k=2 (2,0)='Y', k=3
  k=3 (3,0)='Y', k=4. STOP.
  return 'Y'

sections.why: The first trace shows the early-break behavior — most cells have nothing interesting and the OOB or mismatch fires on k=1. The second shows the 'win exists, found on first scan-direction-pair' happy path. The third confirms the ↑ direction works (which is easy to bug if you accidentally write `[1,0]` as `[-1,0]` thinking 'up means decreasing row'). Tracing all three exposes the row-orientation invariant the candidate picked in section 1.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me walk through edges:
• **Dropping into a full column** — the `for (let r = 0; r < rows; r++)` exits without placing. The `return -1` sentinel signals 'refused' to the caller. If you forget this return, the function returns `undefined`, which the caller probably misreads as 'row 0'.
• **Calling `winner()` on a fresh empty board** — every cell is `''`, the `if (!v) continue` short-circuits every iteration. Returns ''. Constant work, no edge bugs.
• **Diagonal starting from the edge** — say a ↗ diagonal starting at column 4 wants to reach column 8, which is OOB. The `nc >= cols` check inside the while breaks cleanly. The 4-direction limit means we can't detect a ↙ line starting from a high column, but the same line is detected from its other end as ↗.
• **Diagonal that wraps off two edges** — say ↘ from (3, 5) on a 6×7 board: k=1 (4,6) ok, k=2 (5,7) OOB. Breaks before false-match. The bounds check is per-step, not per-direction, which is what saves it.
• **Same color, longer than 4** — 5 in a row should still return that color. Our `while (k < 4)` stops at exactly 4, doesn't keep counting. Fine — we don't need the full length, just 'at least 4'.
• **Multiple wins at once** — a clever drop creates both a horizontal AND vertical 4-line simultaneously. The scan returns whichever it finds first (top-to-bottom, left-to-right, with horizontal direction first). Either is correct — there's only one winning color in legal play."
sections.why: The full-column drop is the most-asked follow-up — interviewers want to hear you defend the -1 sentinel out loud. The diagonal-from-edge case demonstrates that the bounds check is *inside* the while loop (per-step), not a precondition — that's a subtle implementation detail worth voicing. The 'longer than 4' case is a sanity check that the early break-at-4 isn't a bug.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time:
• `drop(col, color)` — O(rows), one column scan to the first empty slot. Strictly bounded by board height.
• `winner()` — O(rows × cols × 4 directions × 4 steps) = O(rows × cols). For a 6×7 board that's 42 × 16 = 672 ops, completely fine.

Space is O(rows × cols) for the board itself; the winner check is O(1) auxiliary.

If the board were huge and `winner()` were called frequently, I'd switch to the after-drop local check — pass the just-dropped `(r, col)` into `winner` and probe only the 4 lines through that cell. That's O(1) per drop, at the cost of coupling the two methods. Same pattern as Tic-Tac-Toe's incremental check.

The broader template — scan-cells-then-probe-directions — generalizes to Word Search II, Gomoku, ship-detection in Battleship. Once you have the 4 direction vectors, the rest is mechanical."
sections.why: Naming the after-drop local-check as the 'next optimization if asked' is the senior move — you've shown you can implement the clean version, and you know exactly what you'd change if pushed. The complexity defense is straightforward (no amortization tricks needed), so the wrap-up's job is mostly to demonstrate transferability via the Word Search / Battleship connection.

walkthrough.intro: Step through a sequence of Connect Four operations on the 6x7 board. drop() finds the lowest empty row and returns it; winner() scans every cell × 4 direction vectors for a 4-in-a-row. The trace collects every drop's row + every winner's color into a results array.

examples.label: drop col 0 (R), col 1 (Y), winner → '' (no four yet)
4×R bottom row cols 0-3 → horizontal R wins
4×Y stacked in col 0 → vertical Y wins

trace: const board = Array.from({ length: rows }, () => new Array(cols).fill(''));
yield { line: 2, label: `new ConnectFour() — empty 6x7 board`, state: { ops, board: board.map(r => r.slice()), results: [...results] } };
yield { line: 7, label: `op#${opIdx}: drop(col=${col}, color='${color}')`, state: { ops, board: board.map(r => r.slice()), results: [...results], col, color } };
yield { line: 9, label: `row ${r} of col ${col} is empty → place '${color}'; return ${r}`, state: { ops, board: board.map(r => r.slice()), results: [...results], col, color, placedR: r } };
yield { line: 11, label: `col ${col} full — return -1`, state: { ops, board: board.map(r => r.slice()), results: [...results], col, color } };
yield { line: 13, label: `op#${opIdx}: winner() — scan every cell × 4 directions`, state: { ops, board: board.map(r => r.slice()), results: [...results] } };
yield { line: 18, label: `cell (${r},${c})='${v}' — probe 4 directions`, state: { ops, board: board.map(r => r.slice()), results: [...results], r, c, v } };
const nr = r + dr * k, nc = c + dc * k;
if (nr < 0 || nr >= rows || nc < 0 || nc >= cols) break;
yield { line: 29, label: `4-in-a-row found from (${r},${c}) in dir ${dirName} — winner='${v}'`, state: { ops, board: board.map(r => r.slice()), results: [...results], r, c, v, dir: dirName, k } };
yield { line: 33, label: `winner() returns '${won}'`, state: { ops, board: board.map(r => r.slice()), results: [...results], won } };
yield { line: 33, label: `all ops processed — results=${JSON.stringify(results)}`, state: { ops, board: board.map(r => r.slice()), results: [...results], returns: JSON.stringify(results) } };

notes: Pick a row convention and stick with it. Here row 0 = bottom; drop scans 0 → rows-1 finding the first empty slot.
Only 4 direction vectors are needed (→, ↑, ↗, ↘) — checking the reverse directions would double-count every line.
After the move you can scan the whole board, OR check only the 4 lines through the just-dropped cell. The full scan keeps the API decoupled.
Time O(rows) per drop, O(rows × cols) per full-board winner(). Space O(rows × cols).

alternates.label: 8-direction local check from the dropped piece
alternates.when: Reach for this if you haven't memorized the 4-mirror optimization, or if `winner()` is called immediately after every `drop` so you can pass in the just-dropped cell. Couples `drop` and `winner` (the win-check needs the landing row), but cuts per-move work from O(rows·cols) to O(1) — only the 4 lines through the new piece can possibly have just completed a 4-in-a-row.
notes: 8 explicit direction vectors paired into 4 line-axes — `(0,1)+(0,-1)` is the horizontal line, `(1,1)+(-1,-1)` is the ↘↖ diagonal, etc. Conceptually simpler than 'only 4 because reverses are redundant'.
Walks outward from the dropped cell in both directions, summing matches; `count >= 4` (not `=== 4`) handles the 5-in-a-row edge cleanly.
Caches `this.won` on the dropped cell so `winner()` becomes O(1) — but the trade is that `drop` and `winner` are no longer independent (the check must run at drop time).

questions.q: Why only check 4 direction vectors (→, ↑, ↗, ↘) instead of all 8?
options: Gravity makes the ↙ and ↘ diagonals impossible to form
The reverse direction of any 4-in-a-row would re-detect the same line from its other end
Only the 4 directions where dr+dc is non-negative produce valid grid moves
Counting in both directions from each cell would double the cap from 4 to 8
questions.explain: The double loop starts a scan from EVERY cell, so any run of four is walked outward from whichever end the row-major scan reaches first. Adding ←, ↓ and the reverse diagonals would just find each of those same lines a second time.

questions.q: Where does a dropped piece land?
options: The topmost cell of the column
The same row as the last opponent piece dropped
The lowest empty row of that column
The next column over if the chosen column is full
questions.explain: `drop` scans `r` from 0 upward and claims the first `''` slot, and this board is built with row 0 as the BOTTOM — so the piece settles on top of whatever is already stacked in that column.

questions.q: What does the inner `while (k < 4)` loop count?
options: Total pieces of color `v` anywhere on the board
How many consecutive cells in this direction match the starting color, capped at 4
Cells of color `v` in the entire row, capped at 4
Steps until the next opponent piece appears in this direction
questions.explain: `k` starts at 1 because the origin cell already counts, then increments once per matching cell along `[dr, dc]`. The two `break`s — out of bounds, or `board[nr][nc] !== v` — are what make the count consecutive rather than a tally of that color anywhere in the line.

options: It signals the piece settled below row 0 — the overflow row
Row index after subtracting 1 for 0-based correction
It's the index returned when the column index is out of bounds
questions.explain: The success path returns the landing row, and valid rows are 0..5 — so -1 is the one value that can't be mistaken for a real answer. Returning 0 on failure would be indistinguishable from 'landed on the bottom row'.

L3.prompt: Implement ConnectFour with drop(col, color) and winner(). Play a sequence that ends with Red completing a ↗ diagonal at (0,0)-(1,1)-(2,2)-(3,3); log winner() before and after the final move.
hints: drop() walks r = 0 upward, settling on the first empty row in the column.
winner() scans every cell; from each non-empty cell try 4 direction vectors (→, ↑, ↗, ↘) and count up to 4 matches.
Return value's truthy color string ('R' or 'Y') when a 4-line is found, '' otherwise.
